security_spec.violation_condition: FreeBSD bhyve VMM sets HENVCFG_STCE to expose stimecmp to VS-mode guests but never saves/restores vstimecmp across VM transitions. When vstimecmp from a prior guest is stale and (time + htimedelta) exceeds it, hardware asserts VSTIP for the incoming guest who did not request it. Conversely, a prior guest's vstimecmp far in the future suppresses a legitimate timer interrupt the incoming guest expects. The spec mandates VSTIP = hvip.VSTIP OR vstimecmp_timer_signal, so both sources must agree; bhyve's dual-track injection (callout-driven HVIP writes AND hardware vstimecmp) creates a conflict where VSTIP can be asserted by vstimecmp after hvip.VSTIP is cleared, or vice versa.
security_spec.summary: bhyve guest stimecmp CSR state leaks across VM boundaries because vstimecmp is not saved/restored on VM transitions even though HENVCFG_STCE is set to enable direct VS-mode access

findings.finding: HENVCFG_STCE is written to henvcfg, enabling VS-mode direct stimecmp access and hardware-driven VSTIP assertion via vstimecmp comparison. However, vstimecmp is never saved/restored across VM transitions (missing from both hypcsr struct and save/restore functions). A prior guest's vstimecmp value persists in hardware across VM switches, causing spurious or suppressed timer interrupts for the incoming guest.

vCPU CSR restore saves 9 CSRs (vsstatus, vsie, vstvec, vsscratch, vsepc, vscause, vstval, hvip, vsatp) but omits vstimecmp. When HENVCFG_STCE is active, the incoming guest inherits the prior guest's stale vstimecmp hardware state, causing hardware to assert VSTIP based on the wrong guest's timer.

vCPU CSR save captures 9 CSRs but omits vstimecmp. The outgoing guest's vstimecmp is never stored, making it impossible to restore later. On next VM entry on this physical CPU, the stale hardware vstimecmp persists.
The hypcsr struct has no vstimecmp field. Even if save/restore CSRs functions were updated, there is no storage allocated for vstimecmp state. This is the root data-structure gap.

Dual-track VSTIP conflict: riscv_sync_interrupts() manages HVIP_VSTIP solely via the host-callout-driven interrupts_pending flag. It clears HVIP_VSTIP when interrupts_pending is 0. However, per the RISC-V spec, VSTIP = hvip.VSTIP OR vstimecmp_timer_signal. The hardware vstimecmp mechanism independently asserts VSTIP regardless of the hvip CSR bit, so clearing hvip.VSTIP does not actually suppress a pending hardware vstimecmp interrupt.

vtimer_set_timer implements a host-callout-based virtual timer (Track 1), clearing interrupts_pending (line 112) when a future timer is set, and scheduling a callout to set interrupts_pending later. This operates entirely on the host-callout path and never touches vstimecmp. Meanwhile, if the guest directly writes stimecmp via the SSTC CSR (Track 2), vstimecmp is updated in hardware without vtimer_set_timer knowing, creating a split-brain between the two timer injection tracks.

Existing TODO comment explicitly acknowledges the race window: a timer interrupt from the previous VM could fire between interrupt synchronization and VM entry. This comment confirms the developers are aware of the issue but have not implemented a fix.

findings.finding: hideleg delegates IRQ_TIMER_HYPERVISOR (bit 5) to VS-mode. Combined with HENVCFG_STCE enabling hardware vstimecmp, this means any spurious VSTIP asserted by stale vstimecmp will be delivered directly to the guest as a timer interrupt — the hypervisor has no opportunity to intercept and suppress it.
